title: Skandamata, Mother of Skanda
hookLine: night five: dolls climb a set of steps in a living room, and the goddess of the night is a mother with her child on her lap
carry: fierce and tender belong to one goddess

cards: In a living room in Chennai, someone has built a staircase out of planks and covered it with a cloth.

On the steps stand dolls: gods near the top, saints and sages lower, then a wedding procession, a market, a cricket match, tiny clay animals. On the floor, a child has made a park out of sand, with a mirror for a pond.
In parts of South India this is the golu, or kolu, set up for Navaratri. In the evenings neighbors come to see it, someone sings, and visitors leave with a small gift.
And tonight, the fifth name in the Kavacha's list is a mother holding her child.

teach.b: Her name is Skandamata, the mother of Skanda.

Skanda is the son of Shiva and Parvati, a young warrior god, known in the Tamil country as Murugan and elsewhere as Kartikeya, and his birth is a story of its own: the demon Taraka could be killed only by a son of Shiva, so the gods waited on that child, and he grew up to lead their army and win.
In paintings of this night his mother sits with the boy on her lap. Notice what the name does. It doesn't call her by her own power.

teach.h: CALLED BY THE CHILD SHE HOLDS.
teach.b: It calls her by the child she holds. And here's the teaching: in Hindu devotion the goddess who rides a lion into battle and the mother with a baby on her lap are not two goddesses. They're one.
The fierce one is fierce for her children; the tender one is strong enough to have raised a god's general. The golu steps make a similar point with dolls.

teach.h: THE WHOLE WORLD ON THE STEPS.
teach.b: Gods at the top, then weddings, vegetable sellers, schoolchildren and cows: the whole ordinary world on the stairs, and neighbors come in to look.
A festival about the goddess turns out to be full of visiting, feeding and children. A good end to a week that began with the goddess giving away her names, and ending them on mother.
Halfway through the nine nights, the lesson so far: the power that clears the road is also the power that holds you.

how: In parts of South India, families set out a golu (kolu or bombe habba), a display of dolls on steps, for Navaratri and visit each other's homes in the evenings; where the nine forms are kept, the fifth night honors Skandamata.

games.q: it's a Navaratri evening in Chennai and a neighbor has invited you to see her golu. what happens when you leave?
o: you're asked to buy a doll for next year.
you're given a small gift to take home.
you're asked to add a doll to the steps.
games.why: visitors leave with a small gift. the festival is full of visiting and feeding, not only worship.

practice: Bring to mind someone who looked after you when you were small, or someone who looks after you now, and stay with one moment of being cared for: a hand on your back, a plate put in front of you.
Then, if it comes easily, let it turn around, and think of someone you hold, in whatever way you hold them. If you pray, you can offer both of them to the goddess, or to God, in your own words.
